page: Vultr vx1-g-2c-8g is an entry-tier general-purpose cloud compute instance configured with 2 dedicated vCPUs mapped to 1 physical AMD EPYC core running at 2.0 GHz, paired with 8.0 GB of system memory and 1 GB of local NVMe SSD storage. The x86_64 processor includes 32 MB of L3 cache alongside support for vector and cryptographic instruction sets, including AVX-512, AVX512_VNNI, AVX512_BF16, and VAES. Network connectivity includes a single complimentary public IPv4 address, and no discrete GPUs are provisioned.

Benchmark results highlight strong single-threaded performance against aggregate multi-threaded limits. In single-core execution, stress-ng scored 3688.67 points, placing it in the top 10 percent of recorded instances. Similarly, single-threaded data compression demonstrated high throughput, with gzip compression reaching 39.96 GB/sec and bzip3 decompression achieving 17.65 GB/sec. Conversely, overall multi-core computational throughput is constrained by the two-thread ceiling, reflected in a bottom-quartile Geekbench multi-core score of 2354.0 and a PassMark CPU score of 4978.82. Uncached memory read bandwidth measured 29.73 GB/sec, while write operations reached 28.99 GB/sec.

The primary hardware tradeoff stems from the restricted 1 GB local NVMe storage allocation, which functions strictly for core system overhead rather than substantial data storage or local database files. Database benchmarks reflect these constraints, with PassMark database operations ranking in the bottom 10 percent and Redis SET throughput recording 3.96 million operations per second. In addition, machine learning workloads are constrained; CPU-based text generation for a 7B parameter model achieved 6.31 tokens per second.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the instance provides dedicated AMD EPYC CPU threads and a balanced 1:4 vCPU-to-RAM memory profile without the overhead of oversized compute pools. The configuration is technically matched to lightweight single-threaded microservices, static web serving (measuring 8.04 GB/sec throughput), compression tasks, edge proxying, and basic automation pipelines that do not depend on substantial local storage.
